title: OST2 Arch1001 20: Binary Bomb Lab and Conclusion (part 1 of 2)

questions.q: You have a binary and want to find the input it expects. Running objdump on it produces a large amount of assembly. What approach does the walkthrough recommend for software that is not known to be malware?
choices: Read the entire disassembly top to bottom before running anything
Use dynamic analysis (run it under a debugger) whenever possible, combined with targeted static reading
Brute-force inputs until one stops the explosion
Only use the strings tool, since all answers appear there in plain text
questions.explain: Pure static analysis doesn't scale well: most real programs are far bigger than the bomb. When it is safe, run the code under a debugger and watch it, and read only the static code you need. In practice you end up using both.

questions.q: In which situation might you choose NOT to do dynamic analysis of a binary?
choices: When the binary has symbols
When the binary is legitimate software you are auditing for vulnerabilities
When the binary is malware, because running it could infect your own system
When the binary reads input from a file
questions.explain: Dynamic analysis means executing the code. With malware, that risks infecting yourself. For anything not known to be malicious, dynamic analysis is preferred whenever possible.

questions.q: Trying every possible input string until the bomb stops exploding is a good way to solve a phase.
questions.explain: The space of possible strings is effectively infinite. The right approach is to look at the code, find the condition that avoids explode_bomb, and work out the input that satisfies it.

questions.q: What does running the `strings` utility on an unknown binary give you, and why is it a good first step?
choices: The printable character sequences embedded in the file, such as messages, which can hint at what the program does
A full disassembly of every function
The values of every argument passed to each function at run time
A list of the exact inputs the program will accept
questions.explain: strings dumps readable text found in the binary. For the bomb this showed the welcome banner plus messages like "That's number 2. Keep going!" and "Halfway there!", which tell you how the program progresses. It is a cheap first look.

questions.q: The hints say to "stay focused on your goal." What does that mean for solving a phase?
choices: Understand every instruction in the phase before stepping through it
Identify the exit condition for the level (the path that avoids explode_bomb) and walk backwards from it to the input that satisfies it
Rewrite the phase in C before trying any input
Patch out every call to explode_bomb
questions.explain: You usually don't need to understand all of the code. Find which control-flow path avoids the explosion, then reason backwards about what values (and therefore what input) take that path.

questions.q: phase_1 calls a helper named strings_not_equal. Instead of reading that helper's assembly, what did the walkthrough do?
choices: Set a watchpoint on every byte of the input
Rewrote it as a C function
Treated it as a black box: stepped over the call and looked at the return value in rax
Skipped it with a jump command
questions.explain: phase_1 is short. All that matters is the return value tested right after the call. Stepping over the call with ni and checking eax shows the return value directly, which is faster than reverse engineering the comparison loop.

questions.q: While analyzing a phase, you find a call to an unfamiliar standard library function. According to the hints, what is your best resource?
choices: The Intel instruction manual
The standard C library documentation for that function
The program's printed output
The binary's symbol table
questions.explain: "Standard C library documentation is your friend!" The docs tell you what the arguments mean and what the function returns, so you can treat it as a known black box.

questions.q: In GDB, what is the difference between `si` and `ni`?
choices: si steps one source line; ni steps one assembly instruction
si steps one instruction and goes into called functions; ni steps one instruction but steps over calls
si sets a breakpoint; ni removes it
They are identical aliases
questions.explain: stepi (si) executes one machine instruction and follows a call into the callee. nexti (ni) also executes one instruction, but runs a call to completion and stops at the next instruction in the current function.

questions.q: Which GDB command shows 10 bytes of memory, in hexadecimal, starting at the address held in rdi?
choices: p/x $rdi
x/10xg $rdi
x/10xb $rdi
x/s $rdi
questions.explain: x examines memory: /10 is the count, x is hex format, b is byte-sized units. p/x $rdi prints the register value itself, not the memory it points to. x/10xg would show ten 8-byte giant words. x/s shows a string.

questions.q: You suspect rsi points to a C string. Which GDB command shows it as human-readable text?
choices: x/s $rsi
p $rsi
x/i $rsi
info registers rsi
questions.explain: x/s reads memory at that address as a null-terminated string. p $rsi and info registers rsi only show the pointer value. x/i would decode the bytes as instructions.

questions.q: You want to restart the bomb in GDB and keep control before it reaches any phase. Why use `start` instead of `run`?
choices: start runs faster
start runs the program and stops at a temporary breakpoint at main; run just runs, and without breakpoints the program can carry on to an explosion
run ignores command-line arguments; start does not
start disables explode_bomb
questions.explain: start is like setting a temporary breakpoint on main and then running. With run and no breakpoints, the bomb runs freely, and if you give it wrong input it blows up before you can step through anything.

questions.q: In `gdb bomb -q -x commands`, what does `-x commands` do?
choices: Marks the file as executable
Executes the GDB commands in the file named `commands` at startup (display settings, breakpoints, start, etc.)
Passes `commands` to the bomb as its first argument
Exports the disassembly to a file named `commands`
questions.explain: -x runs GDB commands from a file. This lets you set up displays (next 10 instructions, registers, stack), breakpoints and `start` automatically on every launch. -q (quiet) suppresses the startup banner.

questions.q: Your phase 1 answer is in a.txt. Inside GDB, how do you start the bomb so it reads answers from that file?
choices: start a.txt
start < bomb a.txt
file a.txt
source a.txt
questions.explain: Arguments after start/run go to the program being debugged, so the bomb gets a.txt as argv[1] and fopen()s it. `file` would load a.txt as the executable to debug. `source` would run it as GDB commands.

questions.q: After solving phase 1, why add a breakpoint on phase_2 (with `start a.txt`) to your GDB command file?
choices: So GDB skips phase_2 entirely
So every restart replays the solved phases from the file and stops at the entry of the phase you're working on
Because GDB can't step into a function without a breakpoint on it
So phase_2 receives the contents of a.txt as its argument
questions.explain: Earlier answers come from the file, and the breakpoint drops you straight into the next unsolved phase. You don't have to retype answers or step through solved code on every restart.

questions.q: You use `ni` on the instruction that calls read_line, but GDB doesn't return to its prompt. Why?
choices: GDB crashed
The call hasn't returned yet: read_line is blocked waiting for you to type a line on stdin
ni doesn't work on call instructions
The bomb already exploded
questions.explain: ni runs the whole call until it returns. read_line is waiting for input, so the program sits there until you type something and press Enter. Then GDB stops at the next instruction.

questions.q: Your GDB setup shows only the next 10 instructions. Which command shows the whole function you're stopped in?
choices: disassemble
info frame
backtrace
list
questions.explain: With no argument, disassemble prints the full disassembly of the current function (e.g. main), with a marker at the current instruction. You can also give it a function name, e.g. disassemble phase_1.

questions.q: Under the System V x86-64 calling convention (Linux), which register holds the first integer or pointer argument to a function?
choices: rax
rcx
rsi
rdi
questions.explain: System V passes the first arguments in rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8, r9, in that order. (rcx is the first argument on Microsoft x64, not System V.)

questions.q: Under System V x86-64, which register holds the second argument?
choices: rdx
rsi
rbx
rdi
questions.explain: The order is rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8, r9, so the second argument is in rsi. In phase_1, rsi held the pointer to the bomb's built-in comparison string.

questions.q: After stepping over `call strings_not_equal`, which register do you check for its return value?
choices: rdi
rsp
rax (eax for a 32-bit int)
rip
questions.explain: Integer return values come back in rax. Since the result is an int, the code tests eax, the low 32 bits of rax.

questions.q: Since rdi pointed to your input string right before `call phase_1`, you can be certain phase_1 takes your input as an argument.
questions.explain: phase_1 might take no arguments, and rdi could hold a leftover value: a red herring. Treat it as a hypothesis to test, e.g. by seeing whether the function actually uses rdi.

questions.q: Examining memory at rdi shows the bytes 69 6e 70 75 74 00. Read as ASCII, what string do they spell?
questions.explain: 0x69='i', 0x6e='n', 0x70='p', 0x75='u', 0x74='t', and 0x00 is the null terminator. Viewing the memory as characters (x/c) or as a string (x/s) would have shown this right away.

questions.q: Before the call to strings_not_equal, why is it reasonable to examine both rdi and rsi as strings?
choices: The name suggests it compares two strings, which C passes as two pointers: the first two arguments, in rdi and rsi
rdi and rsi are always string pointers on x86-64
The 'si' and 'di' in the register names stand for 'string input' and 'data input'
strings_not_equal is a GDB built-in that reads those registers
questions.explain: Use the function name to guess its signature (two char* arguments), then use the calling convention to know where those arguments live. Checking with x/s $rdi showed your input, and x/s $rsi showed the expected string.

questions.q: What does `test eax, eax` do?
choices: Compares eax to 1 and stores the result in eax
Computes eax AND eax, discards the result, and sets flags; ZF=1 exactly when eax is 0
Subtracts eax from itself, setting eax to 0
Tests whether eax holds a valid pointer
questions.explain: test works like AND but only updates the flags. A value ANDed with itself is zero only if the value is zero, so test reg, reg is the standard zero check.

questions.q: `jne` (jump if not equal) is the same instruction as which other mnemonic?
choices: jnz (jump if not zero)
jg (jump if greater)
jb (jump if below)
jmp (unconditional jump)
questions.explain: jne and jnz are two names for the same opcode. Both jump when ZF=0.

questions.q: strings_not_equal returns eax = 0, and then `test eax, eax` runs. What is the value of the zero flag (ZF)? (Enter 0 or 1)
questions.explain: 0 AND 0 = 0, so the result is zero and ZF is set to 1. A following jne/jnz is therefore not taken.

questions.q: phase_1 does: `call strings_not_equal`, then `test eax, eax`, then `jne <address of a call to explode_bomb>`. What must strings_not_equal return for the bomb NOT to explode?
choices: Any nonzero value
Exactly 1
A negative value
questions.explain: jne is taken when ZF=0, which happens when eax is nonzero, and that path calls explode_bomb. You want the jump not taken, which needs eax = 0. Then execution falls through to the add/ret that returns safely.

questions.q: With a wrong input, eax was 1 after strings_not_equal returned. What happens next in phase_1?
choices: ZF=1, so the jump is not taken and phase_1 returns
ZF=0, so the jne is taken to the call to explode_bomb
The test instruction raises an exception
eax is reset to 0 and the comparison is retried
questions.explain: 1 AND 1 = 1 is nonzero, so ZF=0. jne/jnz jumps when ZF=0, which sends execution to the explode_bomb call.

questions.q: strings_not_equal returned 1 for a wrong input and 0 for the right one. Why does that make sense given its name?
choices: It returns 'true' (nonzero) when the strings differ and 'false' (0) when they match
It returns the length of the matching prefix
It returns 0 on error and 1 on success
It returns the number of identical characters
questions.explain: The function answers the question "are the strings not equal?" Yes is nonzero, no is 0. So a 0 return means your input matched the expected string, which is the non-exploding path.

questions.q: Skimming main's disassembly, which repeating pattern shows how the bomb is organized?
choices: fopen, phase_N, fclose, repeated for each phase
read_line, then phase_N (called with the line), then phase_defused, repeated for six phases
explode_bomb, then phase_N, repeated until the input is correct
puts, then exit, after each phase
questions.explain: main reads a line, passes it to phase_1, calls phase_defused, prints a message, and repeats this through phase_6. Each phase is a separate check on one line of input.

questions.q: What does the call to fopen near the start of main tell you about the bomb?
choices: It writes a log of explosions to disk
If given a filename argument, it opens that file and reads phase answers from it line by line, instead of from typed input
It loads its expected answers from a configuration file
It opens its own executable to check for tampering
questions.explain: The bomb takes an optional solutions file (e.g. ./bomb a.txt). Lines are read from the file first, so solved phases don't need to be retyped.

questions.q: If the solutions file only holds the phase 1 answer, the bomb defuses phase 1 from the file and then waits for you to type the phase 2 input.
questions.explain: In the walkthrough, a.txt held only the phase 1 answer. Phase 1 was defused from the file, then the bomb prompted for phase 2 input interactively.

questions.q: When rdi was examined at the call to phase_1, GDB labeled the address with the symbol input_strings. What does this suggest?
choices: The phase's expected answer is stored at input_strings
read_line stored the typed line in a global buffer named input_strings, and main passed a pointer into it to phase_1
input_strings is a register alias for rdi
The bomb encrypts the input before storing it
questions.explain: GDB shows the nearest symbol for an address. That address is in the global input_strings buffer, where read_line put your line, which strongly suggests your input is being passed to the phase.

questions.q: In a phase's disassembly, what is the significance of each `call explode_bomb`?
choices: It's the success path you want to reach
It marks a failure path. You need a control-flow path through the phase that never reaches it
It's a debugging helper you can ignore
It only runs if you're in a debugger
questions.explain: Reaching explode_bomb means wrong input. The conditional jumps that lead to it are your exit conditions. Figure out what values avoid them, then work backwards to the input.

questions.q: On Linux, what does running `strip ./bomb` do?
choices: Removes the symbol information (function and variable names like phase_1, explode_bomb), leaving the code itself unchanged
Removes all calls to explode_bomb
Compresses the binary to make it harder to disassemble
Deletes the strings so the strings tool shows nothing
questions.explain: strip removes the symbol table and debug information. The program behaves the same, but the debugger and disassembler can no longer show helpful names, so you must work out each function's purpose from its code.

questions.q: On Windows, how do you make the bomb symbol-less (the counterpart of `strip ./bomb`)?
choices: Delete bomb.pdb, the separate symbol file
Delete bomb.exe.manifest
Run the bomb as administrator
Rename bomb.exe to bomb.bin
questions.explain: Windows toolchains put debug symbols in a separate .pdb (program database) file rather than in the executable. Without it, WinDbg can't resolve function names.

questions.q: Why is it realistic practice to analyze a binary with its symbols removed?
choices: Stripped binaries run faster under a debugger
Real-world targets such as malware won't ship with symbols, so you must infer each function's role from its behavior
Symbols make the calling convention unpredictable
Debuggers can't set breakpoints when symbols are present
questions.explain: Malware authors don't hand you names like strings_not_equal. Without symbols, you set breakpoints by address and infer function roles from their code and the library calls they make.

questions.q: Stripping the bomb's symbols changes its machine instructions, so the phase answers are different afterwards.
questions.explain: strip removes only symbol and debug metadata. The code and data (including the expected strings) are unchanged, so the answers are the same. They're just harder to find.

questions.q: Which of these does the material call professional reverse-engineering "multi-tools" (as opposed to a standalone debugger like gdb or WinDbg)?
choices: IDA
Ghidra
radare2
strings
objdump
questions.explain: IDA, Ghidra and radare2 combine disassembly, analysis and often debugging in one tool. gdb fits Linux-focused work and WinDbg fits Windows. strings and objdump are single-purpose command-line utilities.
